newsitem.title: USA: NYCE cotton ends weaker on USDA acreage survey.
newsitem.headline: NYCE cotton ends weaker on USDA acreage survey.

text.p: NYCE cotton futures closed sharply weaker on the U.S. Department of Agriculture's forecast for planted cotton area, market sources said.
The USDA put 1997 planted area at 14.48 million acres compared to expectations that ranged from 13.7 million to 14.3 million acres.
The forecast prompted early fund and speculative selling which persisted throughout the day, traders said.
Benchmark May closed down 1.48 cents to settle at 71.35 cents per lb, having hit a fresh contract low of 71.05.
Second-position July also hit a contract low of 72.70, but new-crop December held above its contract low of 74.30 cents and settled at 75.35 cents, down 1.09.
Volume was estimated at 20,000 lots compared to Thursday's official 5,276 lots.

Despite the initial shock to the market, prices are not likely to remain sharply down in the near term. Analysts said the USDA typically reduces its estimate by the end of June, when the second acreage survey is released. Expectations for a reduction, they said, could provide support.
"We still expect producers to change their plantings, particularly in the face of stronger corn and soybean prices," Carl Anderson, a cotton marketing specialist with Texas A & M University, said.
He said that growers in Texas and Oklahoma, who said they would plant 2 percent more cotton in 1997 than in 1996 according to the survey, were encouraged by high yields in the previous crop.
The USDA's estimate put total cotton area only 1 percent less than in 1996, with the greatest losses expected in the Delta.
